analysis.one_liner: Lets the FDA temporarily import foreign-made versions of scarce, overpriced older drugs.
analysis.headline: The bipartisan bill, introduced by Sen. Klobuchar with two Republican cosponsors, never received a committee hearing or vote before the 116th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill targets older prescription drugs that have lost their patents but still have few manufacturers, leaving patients with shortages or high prices. It orders the FDA to let importers bring in foreign-made versions of such drugs — as long as the drug is approved abroad, matches the active ingredient of the scarce US version, and the manufacturer commits to seek US generic approval. It also classifies drugs with fewer than five approved sellers as being 'in shortage,' triggering expedited generic reviews and temporary importation, with authority lasting up to three years.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients who rely on older, off-patent drugs that are in short supply or sold at prices with little competitive pressure — such as hospital drugs and older medicines made by only one or two companies. Hospitals and pharmacists would also gain a backup supply channel.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Patients facing drug shortages and high prices

how_it_helps.text: When a lifesaving or life-sustaining drug faces a shortage, the FDA must authorize importation of a foreign-approved version with the same active ingredient, beginning within 60 days of a qualifying application, and may deny importation only for safety or effectiveness reasons.

Drugs in 'marginally competitive' markets — fewer than five commercially available versions, approved for at least 10 years, with expired active-ingredient patents — are treated as being in shortage for purposes of temporary importation and expedited FDA review and inspections.

Importation authority lasts up to three years or until the shortage ends, and the manufacturer must certify an intent to seek generic approval in the US, so competition is rebuilt rather than permanently outsourced.
The FDA must report annually on the number of drugs authorized for temporary importation, adding a measure of oversight.

analysis.who_pays: Manufacturers of older off-patent drugs sold with little competition would face temporary foreign competition on the drugs where they command high prices or hold sole-supply positions. The FDA would take on added review and inspection work without new funding specified in the bill.
analysis.who_pays_short: Brands with little competition on old drugs

drawbacks.text: The FDA can deny importation for safety or effectiveness concerns, but even supporters acknowledge that vetting foreign production runs carries risk; the bill gives the Secretary discretion to refuse importation if a drug's foreign marketing authorization was withdrawn over safety concerns.

Temporary importation treats the symptom rather than the cause: authority ends after three years or when the shortage clears, so if underlying economics keep driving manufacturers out of low-margin drug markets, shortages could recur.
Importation is conditioned on the manufacturer certifying it will seek US generic approval — a step manufacturers could complete slowly, blunting the competitive benefit the bill aims to create.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits are concrete for a well-defined group of patients: people whose older drugs are scarce or price-gouged because the market has only a handful of sellers. The bill is deliberately narrow — temporary, conditioned on foreign approval and US generic filings, with a safety veto — which limits its reach but also limits the downside. The main honest criticism is that it is a stopgap: it relieves shortages without fixing why manufacturers abandon low-margin drugs in the first place.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate health committee in March 2019, and the committee never took it up before the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Amy Klobuchar introduced the Short on Competition Act on March 14, 2019, joined as original cosponsors by Sen. Mike Lee, Sen. Dick Durbin, and Sen. Chuck Grassley.
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions the same day.
The bill gained three cosponsors in total — two Republicans and one Democrat — and no further action was recorded for the remainder of the 116th Congress, which ended January 3, 2021.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Manufacturers of older, off-patent drugs with few competitors keep their sole-supply positions and pricing power, while patients facing shortages gained no relief.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Uncompetitive drug makers kept the status quo

for.name: Sen. Amy Klobuchar
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and led it in the Senate.

against.name: Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions
against.role: Committee of referral; took no action on the bill
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral and never held a hearing, markup, or vote on it during the 116th Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was sponsored by a Democrat with two Republican cosponsors, and its only recorded obstruction was inaction in committee rather than a party-line vote.

industries.industry: Brand-name and sole-source makers of older off-patent drugs
industries.note: These companies profit when an old drug has fewer than five approved sellers and no foreign competition. The bill forces temporary importation and expedited generic review precisely on those drugs, ending the scarcity premium while the shortage or thin market lasts.

Expedited application review and inspections help domestic generic makers enter abandoned markets sooner. But foreign-manufactured versions would compete with them during importation windows, so the bill both helps and pressures the industry.
The bill creates a new lawful pathway to import FDA-approved foreign versions of scarce drugs, a business opportunity that exists only under this legislation.
Drug shortages force hospitals to ration care, delay treatments, and pay premium prices to gray-market resellers. A guaranteed backup importation channel directly reduces that operational risk.
